challenges.hint: Look at the end of the file

Order these by volatility, most volatile first.
items: Network connections and running process table
challenges.why: Registers vanish fastest, then memory, then network state, then disk, then archives.

challenges.q: Order the acquisition workflow for a suspect laptop.
items: Photograph the scene and note the state
Capture memory if the machine is running
Image the drive with a write blocker
Hash the image and verify it matches
challenges.why: Document, capture volatile data, prove the source, acquire, prove the copy.

challenges.q: Order the incident response phases.
challenges.why: The standard cycle, and preparation is what makes the rest possible.

challenges.q: Order these file system sources by how quickly they lose value after an incident.
items: Open file handles and process memory
challenges.why: Open handles die with the process, live logs rotate, archives persist, unallocated space lasts longest.

challenges.q: Order the steps to hash-verify evidence properly.
challenges.why: You prove the original, acquire, then prove the copy matches.

game-injected-process.intro: Given the listing, identify the anomaly.

challenges.q: Which process is suspicious?
a: cmd.exe parent winword.exe, running from Temp
challenges.why: A document reader spawning a shell is a classic macro malware pattern.

challenges.q: A process appears in psscan but not in pslist. Confidence?
a: Almost certainly unlinked deliberately to hide from the process list
challenges.why: Pool scanning finds structures the linked-list traversal no longer reaches, which indicates DKOM hiding.

challenges.q: Which is the strongest indicator of injection?
a: A private memory region marked executable and containing a PE header
challenges.why: Executable private memory with PE structure means code was mapped in rather than loaded from disk.

challenges.q: sshd has three established outbound connections to port 443 on unrelated hosts. Assessment?
a: Anomalous, possible C2 from a hijacked service process
challenges.why: A service with no reason to make outbound web connections doing so is a beacon.

challenges.q: netscan shows a listening port on a host with no corresponding service. Meaning?
a: A hidden or injected listener that no service owns
challenges.why: A socket with no owning service suggests a backdoor.

challenges.q: A process has a parent PID that no longer exists and is running from /tmp. Assessment?
a: Orphaned or deliberately re-parented, worth investigating
challenges.why: An orphan in a temp path is a common persistence pattern.
